title: Hosted API tenant queue deadlock field diary
content:
Summary:
We observed a P0 degradation where a small subset of tenants triggered a multi-stage queueing deadlock in the hosted API request router between the fronting edge, tenant-specific request queues, and the per-pool execution layer. Symptoms started as elevated p95/p99 generation latency for ~0.4% of customers and escalated to 5xx errors when the request queues hit internal backpressure thresholds and the scheduler stopped dispatching. Total impact window: ~39 minutes (2026-10-14 01:07–01:46 UTC).

Impact:
- Affected surface: hosted text generation (non-streaming) endpoints only; streaming endpoints routed to secondary pool unaffected.
- Scope: ~120 tenants (0.4% of active tenants), mostly small/medium traffic customers but with spiky batched bursts.
- User-visible: elevated latencies (p95 up to 6.2s, p99 up to 14.7s), intermittent 502/503 responses observed from edge.
- Business: brief spike in support tickets and a few automatic client retries; no lasting data loss.

Detection and Alerts:
- First alert: automated p99-latency-on-hostedapi rule fired at 01:09 UTC (2 minutes after first slow request).
- On-call opened incident channel at 01:11 UTC.
- Secondary signal: queue_depth_per_tenant (custom metric) increase noted at 01:12 UTC.

Initial Mitigation Actions (real-time):
- 01:13 UTC: On-call (Ethan) disabled adaptive-batching for the affected pool to reduce large multi-request aggregation. Immediate partial improvement but queueing persisted.
- 01:20 UTC: Traffic reroute applied for tenants with highest queue depth to a warmed spare pool (manual route policy). This reduced error surface by ~60%.
- 01:34 UTC: Short-term throttle introduced at the API gateway for tenants with >50 concurrent inflight requests; this stabilized queue admission and allowed scheduler to drain.
- 01:46 UTC: Incident declared resolved for majority of traffic; gradual rollback of emergency throttles by 02:10 UTC.

Timeline (reconstructed):
- 01:06:50 UTC: First anomalous long-running request (large prompt + high max_tokens) enters pool A.
- 01:07:30 UTC: A micro-burst from a particular tenant group submits ~120 requests within 30s with sticky session routing to pool A.
- 01:08–01:10 UTC: queue_depth_per_tenant metric climbs for ~120 tenants; scheduler begins to prefer local fairness which increases per-tenant queue head-of-line blocking.
- 01:09 UTC: p99 latency alert fires.
- 01:13 UTC: on-call disables adaptive-batching; observed 10–20% latency reduction but queue drain rate insufficient.
- 01:20 UTC: manual tenant reroute to spare pool B implemented.
- 01:34 UTC: emergency throttles at gateway applied to curb fresh admissions.
- 01:46 UTC: backend queues below threshold; return to normal scheduling.

Root Cause Hypotheses (post-incident analysis):
1) Head-of-line blocking due to multi-tenant fairness policy: fairness algorithm attempted to ensure per-tenant minimum throughput by holding slots open for tenants with queued requests, which prevented batch formation and caused inefficient resource utilization when some queued requests were long-running.
2) Adaptive-batching + sticky routing amplification: adaptive-batching tried to group requests, but sticky routing meant large bursts from one tenant were concentrated on a single pool and produced oversized batches that consumed scheduler slots for long durations.
3) Insufficient cross-tenant overflow routing: fallback routing that should spill tenants to spare pools had a conservative threshold and relied on delayed telemetry, so reaction lagged under sudden micro-bursts.
4) Telemetry blind spot: queue_depth_per_pod was visible, but queue_depth_per_tenant had coarse resolution (1m rollup) which masked fast micro-burst growth and delayed automated routing decisions.

Contributing Factors:
- Recent deploy (2026-10-10) tightened fairness time windows to reduce noisy-neighbor effects; regression tolerated steady-state but reduced scheduler agility under bursts.
- No synthetic load tests that exercise tenant-local micro-bursts with sticky routing + adaptive batching.
- Runbook lacked clear steps for emergency tenant reroute and throttle thresholds.

Root Cause (determination):
Primary cause: interplay between per-tenant fairness holding slots open and adaptive-batching + sticky routing concentrating burst traffic on a single pool. Secondary cause: slow telemetry resolution and conservative overflow routing thresholds.

What worked:
- Manual reroute to spare pool worked quickly to restore capacity for the worst-hit tenants.
- Emergency throttles at gateway effectively prevented new inflight growth and let scheduler drain.
- Dashboarding on p99/p95 + per-tenant queue depth (despite coarse rollup) allowed SRE to triage.

What didn’t work / Observed weaknesses:
- Automated overflow did not trigger fast enough due to telemetry rollup and threshold settings.
- Adaptive-batching disabling required manual action and did not recover queue drain rate alone.
- Runbook steps for per-tenant emergency actions were missing, increasing MTTR.

Immediate (short-term) remediation (implemented):
- Increase telemetry frequency for queue_depth_per_tenant from 60s to 10s for high-risk pools (temporary sampling tweak) — completed 2026-10-15.
- Lower overflow routing threshold and enable a fast-path overflow trigger (config change) — staged 2026-10-16, enabled for Canary rings.
- Add a temporary guardrail in gateway to autothrottle tenants with >40 concurrent inflight requests (disabled by default, enabled when queue depth spike detected by high-frequency telemetry) — rolled out 2026-10-16.

Planned permanent fixes (owners & timeline):
- SRE / Serving runtime: Rework fairness policy to avoid holding slots open when queue head-of-line request expected runtime > 2s (Owner: Ethan Park, target: 2026-11-10).
- Serving runtime: Add preemptible slot concept so long-running batches can be demoted to background if head-of-line blocking detected (Owner: Aria Chen, target: 2026-12-01).
- Platform engineering: Implement rapid per-tenant overflow routing that uses high-frequency telemetry and predictive burst detection (Owner: Maya Gomez, target: 2026-11-24).
- Developer-experience: Update client SDK guidance to recommend randomized routing keys when possible to avoid sticky concentrated bursts (Owner: Product SDK team, target: 2026-12-05).

Runbook draft (emergency steps to add to SRE playbooks):
1) Detection: If p99 > 3s and queue_depth_per_tenant delta > 30 in 20s window, escalate to P1/P0.
2) Immediate mitigation (first 10 mins): a) Disable adaptive-batching on affected pool; b) Mark pool as no-new-heat (prevent new sticky sessions); c) Open incident channel and tag serving-runtime and platform engineering.
3) Secondary mitigation (10–30 mins): a) Identify top 10 tenants by queue depth and reroute using manual route policy to spare pool(s); b) If manual reroute not available, activate gateway autothrottle for tenants >40 inflight.
4) Recovery: Wait for pool drain below low-watermark (queue depth <5 per tenant), re-enable batching with observation, then gradually return routing policies.
5) Post-incident: Create ticket for telemetry frequency investigation and schedule root-cause follow-up.

Monitoring and runbook instrumentation additions (to implement):
- Add high-frequency (10s) queue_depth_per_tenant metric flagged for alerting.
- New alert: rapid-tenant-queue-growth (delta > 30 in 20s).
- Add dashboard panel for per-pool tenant fanout distribution and top N tenants by concurrent inflight.

Action items (tracked):
- SRE-4123: Fairness policy quick patch + canary (Ethan Park) — due 2026-11-10.
- SRE-4124: Telemetry sampling increase + alert tuning (Maya Gomez) — due 2026-10-22 (done for canary pools).
- SRE-4125: Implement fast overflow routing prototype (Maya Gomez & Aria Chen) — due 2026-11-24.
- DOC-1077: Runbook update and checklist (Sofia Patel) — due 2026-10-27.

Postmortem notes / decisions for follow-up meeting:
- Accept that fairness optimizations can harm agility; scope tradeoff analysis before tightening fair windows in future deploys.
- Schedule a synthetic load test that replicates tenant-local microbursts with sticky routing and adaptive-batching enabled (owner: SRE + QA).
- Review gateway autothrottle semantics and ensure opt-in for critical customers to avoid unintended throttling.

On-call observations (captured):
- Communication: Incident lead stepped through decisions quickly; cross-team handoffs could be smoother (some delays in platform team acknowledgement).
- Tooling pain: Manual tenant reroute requires console access and takes ~3–7 minutes per tenant; needs automation.

Appendix: Helpful queries and dashboards used during incident
- Query: sum(rate(requests_inflight[10s])) by (tenant_id, pool) — used to find hot tenants.
- Query: increase(queue_depth_per_tenant[20s]) > 30 — rapid-growth detector.
- Dashboard panels: pool capacity vs. active threads, top-25 tenants by inflight, queue age histogram.

Slack / comms snippets:
- 01:12 @oncall: "Seeing p99 spike; queue_depth_per_tenant rising for pool-a-01; investigating batch formation"
- 01:20 @Ethan: "We are routing tenants 12/18 to pool-b as emergency; traffic should recover in ~3–5min"
- 01:36 @Maya: "Autothrottle applied, inbound rate down 70%, scheduler drain observed"

Appendix B: Lessons learned (short bullets)
- Avoid overly rigid fairness windows that block quick reallocation during sudden bursts.
- High-frequency telemetry for tenant-scoped signals is critical for automated control loops.
- Provide simple escape valves (automated reroute, autothrottle) that can be run by on-call without cross-team tickets.

Status: in_review — this is a working post-incident draft. Please add corrections, missing timestamps, and link PRs for the fairness and overflow changes.

Owners for comments: @Sofia (primary author), @Ethan (fairness), @Maya (telemetry/alerting), @Aria (runtime changes)

End of document.
